newsitem.title: FRANCE: French lawmaker offers way out on immigration bill.
newsitem.headline: French lawmaker offers way out on immigration bill.

text.p: A veteran Gaullist parliamentarian offered an amendment to a fiercely contested French immigration bill on Wednesday removing an obligation on citizens and mayors to report on the presence of foreigners.

The amendment by Pierre Mazeaud, chairman of the National Assembly's legislation committee, was aimed at rescuing Prime Minister Alain Juppe's conservative government from a torrent of protests by artists, intellectuals and students.

Thousands of members of France's academic, professional and artistic elite had signed appeals condemning the bill, which would have required citizens to report to the police when a foreign guest left their home.
The bill is aimed at tightening up controls to prevent Third World citizens on short-term tourist visas from overstaying and working illegally in France.
Critics accuse the government of borrowing from the policies of the extreme-right National Front in a bid to win back voters.
Some of the petitions advocated civil disobedience, comparing the measure to the obligation to denounce the presence of Jews during the Nazi occupation of France.
Big demonstrations are planned in Paris on Thursday, Saturday and next Tuesday, the day parliament is due to give the legislation a second reading.
Mazeaud proposed that government prefects rather than local mayors should be responsible for issuing "accommodation certificates" to foreigners subject to visa requirements.
The foreigner himself would have to hand in the form to an immigration official on leaving the country.

"This procedure is designed to remove the legal and practical difficulties posed by the initial draft, while giving the state the means to check that recipients of certificates do not overstay their visas," Mazeaud said.
He said the bill would otherwise have been struck down by the Constitutional Council, France's constitutional watchdog.
After standing by the bill in statements at the weekend, Juppe indicated in parliament on Tuesday he was willing to climb down on the most controversial parts of the legislation.
He said the government was "open to discussion" if lawmakers suggested an alternative way of checking that foreigners really did leave the country when their visas expired.

Francois Leotard, leader of the centre-right Union for French Democracy, junior partners in Juppe's coalition, said in a radio interview on Wednesday that he would not have reported to the police a foreign guest who left his home.
Referring to the protests by artists and intellectuals, Leotard told Europe-1 radio: "I think we have to listen to those people and not treat their action with arrogance."
He denied that Juppe had backed down, saying the government stuck to its objective of clamping down on illegal immigration.
